items.title: Focus Question: Why is it easier to open a heavy door by pushing near its edge than near its hinges?

body.html: The door is 0.90 m wide. You push perpendicular to the door with 15 N, once at the edge and <sub>once 0.20 m from the hinges. Compare the effects.</sub>

ork</sub><sub>: Both pushes are perpendicular, so </sub>sin90° = 1<sub>.</sub> 𝜏<sub>edge</sub> = (15 N)(0.90 m) = 13.5 N·m,

items.title: Explain why r sin θ is the lever arm

body.html: A force acts at the end of a 0.45 m crowbar, at θ = 30° to the bar. Explain why the lever arm is 𝑟sin𝜃<sub> and find it.</sub>

The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of the force. Extend the force's line, then draw <sub>a perpendicular from the axis to that line. This makes a right triangle whose hypotenuse is r (axis to the point where the force</sub> <sub>acts) and whose angle at the point of application is θ, the angle between the force and r. The side opposite θ is the lever arm,</sub> <sub>and opposite = hypotenuse × sin θ.</sub>

answer.html: wer:</sub><sub> </sub>𝐿= 𝑟sin𝜃<sub> because the lever arm is the side opposite θ in a right triangle whose hypotenuse is r. For the crowbar,</sub> 𝐿= 0.225 m<sub>, half of r.</sub>

items.title: Net torque investigation, CCC: Systems and System Models (a coin balance on a meter stick)

body.html: A uniform meter stick is balanced on a pivot at its center. Each coin has the same mass (5.0 g). <sub>Predict which arrangements balance.</sub>

ing</sup><sup>: Net torque about the pivot is </sup>𝜏<sub>net</sub> = 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>1</sub>𝑟<sub>1</sub> −𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>2</sub>𝑟<sub>2</sub><sup>, and the stick stays level only if </sup>𝜏<sub>net</sub> = 0<sup>. The weights are equal and the distances are equal, so</sub> <sub>the torques cancel (balanced).</sub> <sup>Model 2: a stack of three coins 6.0 cm to the left. The right side has the larger torque (14.0 > 10.0 for equal weights),</sub> <sub>so the right side drops.</sub>

Balance when 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>1</sub>𝑟<sub>1</sub> = 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>2</sub>𝑟<sub>2</sub><sup>. items.title: 36 (Critical Thinking): A soup can on a tilted ramp, low friction versus rough

body.html: A solid can is released from rest on a ramp tilted 25° above the horizontal. Compare what <sub>happens on a slick wet plastic ramp (almost no friction) and on a rough carpeted ramp. Draw or describe the free-body diagram</sub> <sub>in each case and say whether the can rotates.</sub>

A can spins only when a net torque acts about its center. The weight acts at the center of mass (zero torque about <sub>the center). The normal force is perpendicular to the surface, so for a round can its line passes through the center (zero torque).</sub> <sub>Friction, if present, acts along the surface at the contact point, a distance r from the center, so it does produce a torque.</sub>

<sub>Slick ramp: only weight and the normal force act, and neither has a torque about the center. So α = 0 and the can slides without</sub> <sub>rotating.</sub> <sub>Carpet: friction acts up the slope at the contact point. It exerts a torque τ = f r about the center, so the can gains angular</sub> <sub>acceleration and rolls down the ramp.</sub>

answer.html: On a nearly frictionless ramp no force makes a torque about the can's center, so it slides without spinning. On the <sub>carpet, friction at the contact point (up the ramp) makes a torque about the center, so the can rolls.</sub>

check.html: Friction also reduces the translational acceleration, matching how rolling objects descend more slowly than sliding ones.

items.title: Focus Question: How does force affect rotation?

body.html: A force changes an object's rotation only through its torque, τ = F r sin θ. The net torque produces angular acceleration, α = τ_net/I.

The bigger the force, the farther from the axis it acts (larger lever arm), and the closer to perpendicular it is, the greater the torque. For a given torque, objects with larger moment of inertia (mass farther from the axis) gain angular velocity more slowly.

answer.html: A force affects rotation by exerting a torque. Torque = force × lever arm, and the resulting angular acceleration is 𝛼= 𝜏<sub>net</sub> / 𝐼.

items.title: Explain why r sin θ is the lever arm

body.html: The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of the force. Extend the force's line; draw a perpendicular from the axis to that line. This makes a right triangle whose hypotenuse is r (axis to the point where the force acts) and whose angle at the point of application is θ, the angle between the force and r. The side opposite θ is the lever arm, and by trigonometry opposite = hypotenuse × sin θ.

answer.html: 𝐿= 𝑟sin𝜃 because the lever arm is the side opposite θ in a right triangle whose hypotenuse is r.

items.title: Get It? Variables in L = r sin θ, and in τ = F r sin θ

answer.html: 𝐿 = lever arm (m), the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of the force. 𝑟 = distance from the axis to where the force is applied (m). 𝜃 = angle between the force and the radius from the axis to the point of application. 𝜏 = torque (N·m). 𝐹 = magnitude of the applied force (N). When θ = 90°, sin θ = 1 and the torque is greatest.

body.html: τ = F r sin θ, with sin 90° = 1.

check.html: Less than the 1.6×10² N needed at 60°, as expected, since a perpendicular pull is most efficient.

items.title: 14: Standing on a bicycle pedal (m = 65 kg, pedal 35° above horizontal, 18 cm from the chain-ring center)

body.html: m = 65 kg, r = 0.18 m. The pedal is 35° above the horizontal and the force (your weight) points straight down. Find τ.
τ = F r sin θ where θ is the angle between the force (down) and the radius (35° above horizontal). That angle is 90° − 35° = 55°, and sin 55° = cos 35°.

answer.html: 𝜏= 94 N·m

check.html: Less than the maximum possible, F r = 115 N·m (horizontal pedal), as it should be.

items.title: 15 (Challenge): Torque with the pedal horizontal and with it vertical

body.html: Same weight force, F = 637 N and r = 0.18 m. The angle between the downward force and the crank is 90° when horizontal and 0° (or 180°) when vertical.
Horizontal: 𝜏= (637)(0.18)sin90° = 1.1 × 10<sup>2</sup> N·m (115 N·m) Vertical: 𝜏= (637)(0.18)sin0° = 0

answer.html: Horizontal: about 1.1 × 10<sup>2</sup> N·m (the maximum). Vertical: 0 N·m, because the force passes through the axis and the lever arm is zero.

check.html: This is why you cannot start a bike by pushing straight down when the pedal is at the top or bottom.

items.title: Net torque investigation, CCC: Systems and System Models (the coin-and-pencil balance in Figure 9)

body.html: Net torque about the pivot is τ_net = F_g1 r₁ − F_g2 r₂, and the pencil stays level only if τ_net = 0. Model 1: equal coins, equal distances, so r₁ = r₂ and the torques cancel (balanced). Model 2: add a second coin on one side (F_g1 = 2F_g2). The balance holds only if that side's distance is halved (r₁ = r₂/2). Model 3: equal coins, but shift the pivot toward one end. The side with the longer arm has the larger torque and that side goes down.

answer.html: Prediction rule: the pencil turns toward the side with the larger product (weight × distance). Balance when 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>1</sub>𝑟<sub>1</sub> = 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>2</sub>𝑟<sub>2</sub>. When you test it, the side with the greater torque drops, as the models predict.

items.title: 16: Ashok (43 kg at 1.8 m) and Steve (52 kg) on a seesaw

body.html: m_A = 43 kg, r_A = 1.8 m, m_S = 52 kg. Find r_S for balance.
The seesaw is balanced when the torques are equal: 𝑚<sub>𝑆</sub>𝑔𝑟<sub>𝑆</sub>= 𝑚<sub>𝐴</sub>𝑔𝑟<sub>𝐴</sub>. The factor g cancels.

answer.html: 𝑟<sub>𝑆</sub>= 1.5 m from the pivot, on the opposite side

check.html: Steve is heavier, so he sits closer than Ashok.

answer.html: 2.70 N·m in the counterclockwise direction (opposite the chain's clockwise torque)

check.html: N × m gives N·m.

Rotational equilibrium of the crank and chain wheel. The weight acts straight down at the pedal, so the angle between the weight and the crank is 45.0°. The chain force is tangent to the chain wheel (lever arm 0.0970 m).

items.title: Get It? Moment of inertia of a hoop

answer.html: 𝐼= 𝑚𝑟<sup>2</sup> for a thin hoop of mass m and radius r, about an axis through its center and perpendicular to its plane.

items.title: Figure 12: Which book requires more torque to rotate?

body.html: Rocking the book about its bottom edge puts most of its mass far from the axis. Rocking it about its middle keeps the mass on average closer to the axis.

answer.html: The book held and rocked at its bottom edge (the top book in Figure 12) has the larger moment of inertia, because its mass is on average farther from the axis, so it needs more torque for the same angular acceleration.

items.title: 21: Children moving from 0.3 m to 0.6 m from the center

body.html: Two children of equal mass m, each at r. Ignore the seesaw. How much does I increase when r goes from 0.3 m to 0.6 m?
𝐼= ∑𝑚𝑟<sup>2</sup>, so 𝐼= 2𝑚𝑟<sup>2</sup>.
The increase is 𝛥𝐼= 2𝑚[(0.6)<sup>2</sup> −(0.3)<sup>2</sup>] = 0.54 𝑚, with m in kg and ΔI in kg·m² (it is 3 times the original 𝐼= 0.18 𝑚).

answer.html: The moment of inertia becomes 4 times as large (an increase of 3 times the original, 0.54𝑚kg·m<sup>2</sup> for children of mass m each).

check.html: I scales as r², and doubling r gives 2² = 4.

items.title: 22: Solid ball versus hollow ball of the same diameter and mass

body.html: Moment of inertia depends on how far the mass is from the axis. In the hollow ball all the mass is at the full radius r. In the solid ball, much of the mass is closer to the center.

For a solid sphere 𝐼=<sub> </sub><sup>2</sup> <sub>5</sub>𝑚𝑟<sup>2</sup> (Table 2). A hollow thin-walled sphere has 𝐼=<sup> </sup><sup>2</sup> <sub>3</sub>𝑚𝑟<sup>2</sup> (a standard result, not in the book's table), which is larger.

answer.html: No. The hollow ball has the greater moment of inertia, because all of its mass is at the maximum distance from the axis (I = 2/3 mr² versus 2/5 mr²).

check.html: The limiting case is a hoop (mr²), the largest possible for a given m and r.

(c) Solid sphere: 𝐼=<sub> </sub><sup>2</sup>

body.html: Spheres equally spaced; A is on the left end and C is the middle one. The A to C distance is d = 0.20 m, so the third sphere is 0.40 m from A. Treat each sphere as a point mass m = 0.10 kg, axis perpendicular to the rod.

About A: distances are 0, d, 2d, so 𝐼<sub>𝐴</sub>= 𝑚(𝑑<sup>2</sup> + 4𝑑<sup>2</sup>) = 5𝑚𝑑<sup>2</sup>. About C: distances are d, 0, d, so 𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub>= 𝑚(𝑑<sup>2</sup> + 𝑑<sup>2</sup>) = 2𝑚𝑑<sup>2</sup>. Numbers: 𝐼<sub>𝐴</sub>= (0.10)(0.20<sup>2</sup> + 0.40<sup>2</sup>) = 0.020 kg·m<sup>2</sup>; 𝐼<sub>𝐶</sub>= (0.10)(0.20<sup>2</sup> + 0.20<sup>2</sup>) = 0.0080 kg·m<sup>2</sup>.

items.title: Physics Challenge: Rank the four sphere-and-rod sets by moment of inertia

body.html: Four equal-mass spheres per set, equal spacing d, massless rod. Axes (from the figure): A, along the rod through all the spheres; B, vertical through the leftmost sphere; C, vertical through the second sphere; D, vertical through the midpoint between the second and third spheres.

𝐼= ∑𝑚𝑟<sup>2</sup>, where r is each sphere's distance from the axis (spheres treated as points). Work (in units of 𝑚𝑑<sup>2</sup>): A: all distances 0, so I = 0. B: distances 0, 1, 2, 3 gives 0 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 14. C: distances 1, 0, 1, 2 gives 1 + 0 + 1 + 4 = 6. D: distances 1.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.5 gives 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 = 5.0.

answer.html: Least to greatest: A (0) < D (5.0 md²) < C (6 md²) < B (14 md²).

items.title: 31: Pushing a stationary revolving door

body.html: Maximum torque for the least force needs the largest lever arm: push far from the axis, perpendicular to the door panel.

answer.html: Vijesh should push on the outer edge of a door panel (as far from the central axis as possible), perpendicular to the panel (tangent to the circle of rotation). Pushing near the axis, or along the panel toward the axis, gives little or no torque.

items.title: 36 (Critical Thinking): Ball on a tilted surface, low friction versus rough

body.html: A ball spins only when a net torque acts about its center. The weight acts at the center of mass (zero torque about the center). The normal force is perpendicular to the surface, so on a sphere its line passes through the center (zero torque). Friction, if present, acts along the surface at the contact point, a distance r from the center, so it does produce a torque.

Low friction: only weight and normal force act, and neither has a torque about the center. So α = 0 and the ball slides without rotating. Rough surface: friction acts up the slope at the contact point. It exerts a torque τ = f r about the center, so the ball gains angular acceleration and rolls down the slope.

answer.html: On a nearly frictionless slope no force makes a torque about the ball's center, so it slides without spinning. On a rough slope, friction at the contact point (up the incline) makes a torque about the center, so the ball rolls.

check.html: Friction also slows the translational acceleration, which matches how rolling balls descend more slowly than sliding ones.
